Stated Claim / Post Context:
Number of adolescents in detention falls by 54% in Brazil, Paraguay bans child marriage, Montréal’s green corridor

In today's edition: fewer Brazilian youths are entering juvenile detention facilities, Paraguay has closed a loophole that allowed 16-17-year olds to marry with parental or judicial consent, and an ecological corridor in Canada's second-largest city has become a biodiversity super-hub.

Actual Article Body:
Elizabeth Jacyshyn-Owen | Posted on October 23, 2026 |

Photo: Joshua Gresham/Unsplash (CC0)

In today’s edition: fewer Brazilian youths are entering juvenile detention facilities, Paraguay has closed a loophole that allowed 16-17-year olds to marry with parental or judicial consent, and an ecological corridor in Canada’s second-largest city has become a biodiversity super-hub.

According to new data from the Brazilian Forum on Public Safety, the number of adolescents held in closed juvenile detention facilities has fallen by half in the past ten years. In 2015, there were 26,800 minors in either detention, provisional detention, disciplinary detention, semi-open custody or other protective measures. In 2025, this number stood at 12,200, a 54.5% drop.

Source: Folha de S.Paulo

Paraguay’s Chamber of Deputies has voted to outlaw marriage under 18 with no exceptions, ending the loophole that lets 16- and 17-year-olds wed with parental or judicial consent. A coalition of children’s rights groups counted 6,111 adolescents aged 15-17 in marriages or early unions in 2025, with 5,625 of them were female.

Source: Rio Times

The Thamani Asili programme, which ‌translates to “value of nature” in Kiswahili, will concrete on biodiversity hotspots spanning from the Great Rift Valley to the Maasai Mara which are home to thousands of elephants, rhinos, lions and other species.

Source: Reuters

According to new data from energy think tank Ember, the global electric vehicle boom has displaced approximately 200 million barrels of crude oil, worth $20 billion (€17.82 billion) between March and August 2026. Within this number, EU member states were responsible for roughly $3.1 billion (€2.76 billion).

Source: Euronews

With prices for housing and energy increasing worldwide, a growing number of solutions with legitimate environmental credentials are gaining traction – including prefabricated modular structures, eco-friendly tiny houses built from calamity wood, and Earthship homes.

Source: Deutsche Welle

Makafui Awuku spotted two major issues in his home of Konongo-Odumase: a lot of plastic waste and not enough tables in schools. To tackle both problems at once, he started creating school desks made from upcycled packaging waste that are more durable and comfortable than standards. options.

Source: BBC News

In the face of continued Russian drone strikes, a repair festival taking place in an underground shelter in Chornomorsk is giving residents the chance to fix broken items after the college building where they hold repair cafés was bombed.

Source: Positive News

The certification programme hopes to encourage developers to create better habitats for wildlife alongside clean electricity generation. Launched by Wild Power, the initiative assesses how renewable energy developments protect and improve habitats, giving certification to those that meet its biodiversity standards.

Source: Positive News

At the Wimpole Estate in Cambridgeshire, the last six years have seen a growing number of rare species appear despite the extreme weather conditions, including barbastelle bats, great crested newts and corn buntings.

Source: BBC News

In the middle of Canada’s second-largest city, Montréal’s Mount Royal has become a biodiverse super-hub, largely thanks to a green corridor that uses the narrow ribbon of vegetation along the edges of railway tracks.

Source: Rewilding Magazine
